transcription.tex: A random variable assigns a numerical value to each outcome of an experiment. A discrete random variable takes separate, countable values.
Roll a fair six-sided die. Let $X$ be the number on its uppermost face.
\(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16\\\hline\end{array}\)

shapes.alt: A six-sided die showing one pip on the top face, two on the left and four on the right.

transcription.tex: What does $\mathrm P(X=x)$ tell us? How would you write the probability of rolling a five?
$\mathrm P(X=x)$ is the probability that the random variable $X$ takes the particular value $x$. The shorthand $p(5)$ means $\mathrm P(X=5)=\frac16$.
We will use this distribution to find its long-run mean (the expected value) and its spread (the variance).
Suppose that we throw a single fair die 60 times, and see the following outcomes:

\(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline P(X=x)&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16\\\hline\end{array}\)\par Throw the die 60 times.\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline \text{Frequency}&9&11&10&8&12&10\\\hline\end{array}\)

shapes.alt: A six-sided die showing one pip on the top face, two on the left and four on the right.

transcription.tex: What is the mean outcome based on our sample?
\(\bar x=(1\times9+2\times11+3\times10+4\times8+5\times12+6\times10)/60=213/60=3.55.\)
But using the actual probabilities of each outcome (i.e. 1/6 for each), what would we expect the average outcome to be?
Each face is equally likely, so the expected mean is \((1+2+3+4+5+6)/6=3.5\).
For a discrete random variable \(X\), its expected value is \(E(X)=\sum_x x\,P(X=x)\). This is the long-run mean over many repetitions.
Find the expected value of the following distributions (in your head!).
\(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3\\\hline P(X=x)&0.1&0.6&0.3\\\hline\end{array}\)
\(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline x&4&6&8\\\hline P(X=x)&0.5&0.25&0.25\\\hline\end{array}\)
\(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline x&10&20&30\\\hline P(X=x)&\tfrac14&\tfrac12&\tfrac14\\\hline\end{array}\)
Tip: Suppose you treated the probabilities as frequencies then found the mean of the ‘frequency table’. What do you notice?
Tip: If the outcomes and their probabilities are symmetric about a central value, the expected value equals that central value.
\(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3&4&5\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&0.1&p&0.3&q&0.2\\\hline\end{array}\)
Given that $\mathrm E(X)=3$, find the values of $p$ and $q$.
Hint: Can you think of TWO ways we could get an equation relating $p$ and $q$?
The probabilities add to 1, so $p+q+0.1+0.3+0.2=1$. Hence $p+q=0.4$.\par The expected value gives $0.1+2p+0.9+4q+1=3$. Hence $2p+4q=1$.
Double $p+q=0.4$ to get $2p+2q=0.8$. Subtract this from $2p+4q=1$.\par Then $2q=0.2$, so $q=0.1$ and $p=0.4-0.1=0.3$.

slides.title: Exam style question

transcription.tex: A biased die with six faces is rolled. The discrete random variable \(X\) represents the score on the uppermost face. The probability distribution of \(X\) is shown in the table below.\par \[\begin{array}{c|rrrrrr}x&1&2&3&4&5&6\\P(X=x)&a&a&a&b&b&0.3\end{array}\]\par (a) Given that \(E(X)=4.2\) find the value of \(a\) and the value of \(b\). [5 marks]
Edexcel S1(Old) June 2013 Q5

(a) $3a+2b+0.3=1$, hence $3a+2b=0.7$. [M1]\par $a+2a+3a+4b+5b+1.8=4.2$, so $6a+9b=2.4$. [M1]\par Double the first equation: $6a+4b=1.4$. Subtract it from the second: $5b=1$. [M1]\par $b=0.2$. [B1]\par $3a=0.7-2(0.2)=0.3$, so $a=0.1$. [B1]

slides.navigationTitle: Exam style question · Edexcel S1(Old) June 2013 Q5

transcription.tex: If $X$ is the original random variable, compare the outcomes of $X$, $2X$ and $X^2$.
Original outcomes\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3\\\hline p(x)&0.1&0.4&0.5\\\hline\end{array}\)
Double each outcome\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline 2x&2&4&6\\\hline p(x)&0.1&0.4&0.5\\\hline\end{array}\)
Square each outcome\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline x^2&1&4&9\\\hline p(x)&0.1&0.4&0.5\\\hline\end{array}\)
Each outcome keeps its probability. For instance, $X=3$, $2X=6$ and $X^2=9$ all describe the same event, with probability $0.5$.
How can we find the expected value of the squares from the third table?
\(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline x&-2&0&1\\\hline p(x)&0.3&0.6&0.1\\\hline\end{array}\)
Determine $\mathrm E(X^2)$.
Square each possible outcome before weighting it by its probability.\par \(\mathrm E(X^2)=(-2)^2\times0.3+0^2\times0.6+1^2\times0.1\)\par \(=4(0.3)+0+0.1=1.3.\)
Question 5

The random variable \(X\) has the following probability distribution:\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3&4&5\\\hline P(X=x)&0.1&a&b&0.2&0.1\\\hline\end{array}\)\par Given that \(E(X)=2.9\), find the value of \(a\) and the value of \(b\).

The probabilities sum to 1:\par \(0.1+a+b+0.2+0.1=1\), so \(a+b=0.6.\qquad(1)\)\par Using \(E(X)=\sum_x xP(X=x)=2.9\) gives\par \(1(0.1)+2a+3b+4(0.2)+5(0.1)=2.9.\)\par Thus \(0.1+2a+3b+0.8+0.5=2.9\), or\par \(2a+3b=1.5.\qquad(2)\)\par Multiply equation (1) by 2:\par \(2a+2b=1.2.\qquad(3)\)\par Subtract equation (3) from equation (2) to give \(b=0.3\). Substitute \(b=0.3\) into equation (3): \(2a+0.6=1.2\), hence \(a=0.3\).
Question 6

The random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution:\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&-2&-1&1&2\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&0.1&a&b&c\\\hline\end{array}\)\par Given that $\mathrm E(X)=0.3$ and $\mathrm E(X^2)=1.9$, find $a$, $b$ and $c$.\par \textbf{Problem-solving} You can use the given information to write down simultaneous equations for $a$, $b$ and $c$ which can be solved using the matrix inverse operation on your calculator.

$\mathrm E(X)=\sum_x x\mathrm P(X=x)=0.3$, so\par \(0.3=(-2\times0.1)+(-1\times a)+(1\times b)+(2\times c)\)\par \(0.5=-a+b+2c\quad(1)\)\par $\mathrm E(X^2)=\sum_x x^2\mathrm P(X=x)$, so\par \(1.9=(4\times0.1)+(1\times a)+(1\times b)+(4\times c)\)\par \(1.5=a+b+4c\quad(2)\)\par $\sum_x\mathrm P(X=x)=1$, so\par \(1=0.1+a+b+c\)\par \(0.9=a+b+c\quad(3)\)\par \((2)-(3):\quad 0.6=3c,\quad c=0.2\)\par \((3)-(1):\quad 0.4=2a-c\)\par \(2a=0.4+c=0.6,\quad a=0.3\)\par Substituting for $a$ and $c$ in (3) gives\par \(0.9=0.3+b+0.2,\quad b=0.4\)\par So $a=0.3$, $b=0.4$, $c=0.2$.
Question 7

The discrete random variable $X$ has probability function\par \(\mathrm P(X=x)=\begin{cases}a(1-x)&x=-2,-1,0\\ b&x=5\end{cases}\)\par Given that $\mathrm E(X)=1.2$, find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$.

The probability distribution for $X$ is\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&-2&-1&0&5\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&3a&2a&a&b\\\hline\end{array}\)\par $\mathrm E(X)=\sum_x x\mathrm P(X=x)=1.2$, so\par \(1.2=-2\times3a-1\times2a+0\times a+5\times b\)\par \(1.2=-6a-2a+5b\)\par \(1.2=-8a+5b\quad(1)\)\par $\sum_x\mathrm P(X=x)=1$, so\par \(1=3a+2a+a+b\)\par \(1=6a+b\quad(2)\)\par \((2)\times5:\quad 5=30a+5b\quad(3)\)\par \((3)-(1):\quad 3.8=38a\quad\Rightarrow\quad a=0.1\)\par Substituting for $a$ in (2) gives\par \(b=1-6a=1-0.6=0.4\)\par So $a=0.1$, $b=0.4$.
Question 8

A biased six-sided dice has a $\frac18$ chance of landing on any of the numbers 1, 2, 3 or 4. The probabilities of landing on 5 or 6 are unknown. The outcome is modelled as a random variable, $X$. Given that $\mathrm E(X)=4.1$,\par \textbf{a} find the probability distribution of $X$.\par The dice is rolled 10 times.\par \textbf{b} Calculate the probability that the dice lands on 6 at least 3 times.

\textbf{a} Suppose the probability distribution for $X$ is\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&\frac18&\frac18&\frac18&\frac18&a&b\\\hline\end{array}\)\par $\mathrm E(X)=\sum_x x\mathrm P(X=x)=4.1$, so\par \(4.1=1\times\tfrac18+2\times\tfrac18+3\times\tfrac18+4\times\tfrac18+5a+6b\)\par \(4.1=\tfrac{10}{8}+5a+6b\)\par \(2.85=5a+6b\quad(1)\)\par $\sum_x\mathrm P(X=x)=1$, so\par \(1=\tfrac18+\tfrac18+\tfrac18+\tfrac18+a+b\)\par \(0.5=a+b\quad(2)\)\par \((2)\times 5:\quad 2.5=5a+5b\quad(3)\)\par \((1)-(3):\quad 0.35=b\)\par Substitute $b$ in (2). Then $0.5=a+0.35$, so $a=0.15$.\par \(a=0.15=\tfrac{3}{20},\quad b=0.35=\tfrac{7}{20}.\)\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&\frac18&\frac18&\frac18&\frac18&\frac3{20}&\frac7{20}\\\hline\end{array}\)\par \textbf{b} Let $Y$ count the sixes in ten rolls. Then $Y\sim\mathrm B(10,\tfrac7{20})$. We need $\mathrm P(Y\ge3)$.\par \(\mathrm P(Y\ge3)=1-\mathrm P(Y=0)-\mathrm P(Y=1)-\mathrm P(Y=2).\)\par Use $\mathrm P(Y=r)=\binom nr p^r(1-p)^{n-r}$ with $n=10$ and $p=0.35$. Subtract these three terms from 1:\par \(\mathrm P(Y=0)=\binom{10}{0}0.35^0\,0.65^{10}\approx1\times1\times0.013463\)\par \(\mathrm P(Y=1)=\binom{10}{1}0.35^1\,0.65^9\approx10\times0.35\times0.020712\)\par \(\mathrm P(Y=2)=\binom{10}{2}0.35^2\,0.65^8\approx45\times0.1225\times0.031864\)\par \(\mathrm P(Y\ge3)\approx1-(0.013463+0.072492+0.17565)\)\par \(=1-0.261605\approx0.7384\quad\text{(4 d.p.).}\)
Question 9

Jorge has designed a game for his school fete. Students can pay £1 to roll a fair six-sided dice. If they score a 6 they win a prize of £5. If they score a 4 or a 5, they win a smaller prize of £$P$.\par By modelling the amount paid out in prize money as a discrete random variable, determine the maximum value of $P$ in order for Jorge to not make a loss on his game.\par \textbf{Hint} The expected profit from the game is the cost of playing the game minus the expected value of the amount paid out in prize money.

This is the result of each throw of the dice:\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Score}&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline \text{Probability}&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16\\\hline \text{Prize (£)}&0&0&0&P&P&5\\\hline\end{array}\)\par Let $X$ be the amount paid out in prize money. From the table its distribution is\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline x&0&P&5\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&\frac12&\frac13&\frac16\\\hline\end{array}\)\par $\mathrm E(X)=\sum_x x\mathrm P(X=x)$ is the expected payout.\par \(\mathrm E(X)=0\times\tfrac12+P\times\tfrac13+5\times\tfrac16.\)\par At break-even, expected profit is zero. Expected profit equals the cost of the game minus the expected payout.\par \(0=1-\bigl(\tfrac13P+\tfrac56\bigr)\)\par \(\tfrac13P=\tfrac16\quad\Rightarrow\quad P=0.5.\)\par A prize of £0.50 for a 4 or a 5 gives an expected profit of zero. A larger prize would make the expected profit negative. The maximum prize is £0.50.

slides.title: Variance of a discrete random variable

transcription.tex: Again, imagine that we throw a fair die 60 times, and that we get the ‘expected’ frequencies for each outcome.
\(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16&\frac16\\\hline \text{Frequency}&10&10&10&10&10&10\\\hline\end{array}\)

shapes.alt: A six-sided die showing one pip on the top face, two on the left and four on the right.

transcription.tex: There are ten of each score. The mean is $3.5$, exactly the expected value of the fair die. How far, on average, are the outcomes from their mean when we square the distances?

The squared distances occur in equal pairs. Thus $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\tfrac16\{2(2.5)^2+2(1.5)^2+2(0.5)^2\}=\tfrac{35}{12}$.\par These are the frequencies expected over many repetitions. In a particular set of 60 throws the observed frequencies, and hence the observed variance, can differ.
Average squared distance from the mean
Mean of the squares minus the square of the mean
For a list of $n$ values with mean $\bar x$
\(\sigma^2=\frac{\sum (x-\bar x)^2}{n}\)
\(\sigma^2=\frac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar x^2\)
For a discrete random variable $X$
\(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathrm E\big[(X-\mathrm E(X))^2\big]\)
\(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathrm E(X^2)-[\mathrm E(X)]^2\)
For the definition, subtract the mean from each outcome, square the difference and take its expected value. The equivalent formula on the right usually makes the calculation shorter.
\(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&0.1&0.5&0.4\\\hline\end{array}\)
Find $\mathrm E(X)$ and $\mathrm E(X^2)$ first.
Calculator tip: Enter the outcomes in the data column and their probabilities in the frequency column. The population variance $\sigma^2$ equals $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.

transcription.tex: 3. The discrete random variable \(X\) has probability distribution given by\par \[\begin{array}{c|rrrrr}x&-1&0&1&2&3\\P(X=x)&\frac15&a&\frac1{10}&a&\frac15\end{array}\]\par where \(a\) is a constant.\par (a) Find the value of \(a\).\par (b) Write down \(E(X)\).\par (c) Find \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
Edexcel S1(Old) May 2010
The probabilities sum to 1: \(2a+\frac12=1\), so \(a=\frac14\).
The distribution is symmetric about 1, giving \(E(X)=1\).

transcription.tex: 3. When Rohit plays a game, the number of points he receives is given by the discrete random variable \(X\) with the following probability distribution.\par \[\begin{array}{c|rrrr}x&0&1&2&3\\P(X=x)&0.4&0.3&0.2&0.1\end{array}\]\par (a) Find \(E(X)\).\par (b) Find \(F(1.5)\).\par (c) Show that \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1\).
Edexcel S1(Old) Jan 2009
The cumulative distribution function is $F(t)=\mathrm P(X\le t)$. The scores at or below 1.5 are 0 and 1, so $F(1.5)=0.4+0.3=0.7$.

transcription.tex: Question 6

A fair coin is spun repeatedly until a head appears or three spins have been made. The random variable $T$ represents the number of spins of the coin.\par \textbf{a} Show that the probability distribution of $T$ is\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline t&1&2&3\\\hline \mathrm P(T=t)&\frac12&\frac14&\frac14\\\hline\end{array}\)\par \textbf{b} Find the expected value and variance of $T$.

\textbf{a} A head on the first spin has probability $\frac12$. Hence $\mathrm P(T=1)=\frac12$.\par A tail then a head has probability $\tfrac12\times\tfrac12$, so $\mathrm P(T=2)=\tfrac14$.\par \(\mathrm P(T=3)=1-[\mathrm P(T=1)+\mathrm P(T=2)]=1-(\tfrac12+\tfrac14)=\tfrac14.\)\par Alternatively, the third spin is reached after two tails. Its outcome may be a head or a tail.\par \(\mathrm P(T=3)=\mathrm P(TTH)+\mathrm P(TTT)\)\par \(=\tfrac12\times\tfrac12\times\tfrac12+\tfrac12\times\tfrac12\times\tfrac12=\tfrac18+\tfrac18=\tfrac14.\)\par \textbf{b} $\mathrm E(T)=1\times\tfrac12+2\times\tfrac14+3\times\tfrac14=\tfrac74=1.75$.\par \(\mathrm E(T^2)=1\times\tfrac12+4\times\tfrac14+9\times\tfrac14=\tfrac{15}{4}=3.75.\)\par \(\operatorname{Var}(T)=\tfrac{15}{4}-(\tfrac74)^2=\tfrac{60}{16}-\tfrac{49}{16}=\tfrac{11}{16}=0.6875.\)
Question 7

The random variable $X$ has a probability distribution given by\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline x&1&2&3\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&a&b&a\\\hline\end{array}\)\par where $a$ and $b$ are constants.\par \textbf{a} Write down an expression for $\mathrm E(X)$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.\par \textbf{b} Given that $\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.75$, find the values of $a$ and $b$.

\textbf{a} $\mathrm E(X)=\sum_x x\mathrm P(X=x)=a+2b+3a=4a+2b$.\par \textbf{b} $\sum_x p(x)=1$, so $2a+b=1\quad(1)$.\par \(\mathrm E(X)=4a+2b=2(2a+b)=2.\)\par \(\mathrm E(X^2)=a+4b+9a=10a+4b.\)\par \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathrm E(X^2)-[\mathrm E(X)]^2=10a+4b-2^2=10a+4b-4.\)\par The variance is $0.75$, giving $10a+4b=4.75\quad(2)$.\par Multiply (1) by 4 to get $8a+4b=4\quad(3)$.\par Subtract (3) from (2). Then $2a=4.75-4=0.75$, so $a=0.375$.\par Substitute into (1). From $0.75+b=1$, $b=0.25$.
Suppose that we have a list of people’s heights $x$. The mean height is $\bar x=1.5\,\mathrm m$ and the variance is $\sigma_x^2=0.2\,\mathrm m^2$. We use the coding $y=3x-10$.
$\bar y=3\bar x-10=3(1.5)-10=-5.5$. The mean changes in the same way as each observation.
$\sigma_y^2=3^2\sigma_x^2=9(0.2)=1.8$. Subtracting a constant leaves every distance from the mean unchanged. Multiplying lengths by 3 multiplies their squared distances by 9.
The same rules apply to the expected value and variance of a random variable.
\(\mathrm E(X+10)=\mathrm E(X)+10\)
\(\mathrm E(3X)=3\mathrm E(X)\)
\(\operatorname{Var}(3X)=9\operatorname{Var}(X)\)
Express these in terms of the original \(E\left(X\right)\) and \(Var\left(X\right)\).
\(E\left(4X+1\right)\;=\)
\(4E\left(X\right)+1\)
\(E\left(1-X\right)\;=\)
\(1-E\left(X\right)\)
\(Var\left(4X\right)\;=\)
\(16Var\left(X\right)\)
\(Var\left(X+1\right)\;=\)
\(Var\left(X\right)\)
\(Var\left(3X+2\right)\;=\)
\(9Var\left(X\right)\)
\(E\left(\frac{X-1}{2}\right)\;=\)
\(\frac{E\left(X\right)-1}{2}\)
\(Var\left(\frac{X-1}{2}\right)\;=\)
\(\frac{1}{4}Var\left(X\right)\)

slides.title: Does the same rule hold for sine?

transcription.tex: Is $\mathrm E(\sin X)=\sin(\mathrm E(X))$ in the same way that $\mathrm E(2X)=2\mathrm E(X)$?
\(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|}\hline x&30^\circ&60^\circ\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&0.2&0.8\\\hline\end{array}\)
Take the sine of each angle first, then weight the two results.\par \(\mathrm E(\sin X)=0.2\sin30^\circ+0.8\sin60^\circ=0.792820\ldots\)
Take the weighted mean angle first, then its sine.\par \(\sin(\mathrm E(X))=\sin(0.2\times30^\circ+0.8\times60^\circ)=\sin54^\circ=0.809017\ldots\)
For a nonlinear function $f$, $\mathrm E(f(X))$ can differ from $f(\mathrm E(X))$. We have already seen this with squaring: their difference is the variance.
Question 8

Two tetrahedral dice are rolled. The random variable $X$ represents the result of subtracting the smaller score from the larger.\par \textbf{a} Find $\mathrm E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.\par The random variables $Y$ and $Z$ are defined as $Y=2^X$ and $Z=\dfrac{4X+1}{2}$\par \textbf{b} Show that $\mathrm E(Y)=\mathrm E(Z)$.\par \textbf{c} Find $\operatorname{Var}(Z)$.

\textbf{a} The rows and columns give the two dice scores. Each entry is their difference.\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|}\hline &1&2&3&4\\\hline 1&0&1&2&3\\\hline 2&1&0&1&2\\\hline 3&2&1&0&1\\\hline 4&3&2&1&0\\\hline\end{array}\)\par Count the 16 equally likely outcomes:\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&0&1&2&3\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&\frac{4}{16}&\frac{6}{16}&\frac{4}{16}&\frac{2}{16}\\\hline\end{array}\)\par $\mathrm E(X)=\sum_x x\mathrm P(X=x)$\par \(=0\times\tfrac4{16}+1\times\tfrac6{16}+2\times\tfrac4{16}+3\times\tfrac2{16}=\tfrac{20}{16}=\tfrac54=1.25.\)\par $\mathrm E(X^2)=\sum_x x^2\mathrm P(X=x)$\par \(=0^2\times\tfrac4{16}+1^2\times\tfrac6{16}+2^2\times\tfrac4{16}+3^2\times\tfrac2{16}=\tfrac{40}{16}=\tfrac52=2.5.\)\par \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathrm E(X^2)-[\mathrm E(X)]^2=2.5-1.25^2=2.5-1.5625=0.9375.\)\par \textbf{b} Transform each value using $Y=2^X$:\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&0&1&2&3\\\hline y&1&2&4&8\\\hline \mathrm P(Y=y)&\frac14&\frac38&\frac14&\frac18\\\hline\end{array}\)\par \(\mathrm E(Y)=\sum_y y\mathrm P(Y=y)\)\par \(=1\times\tfrac14+2\times\tfrac38+4\times\tfrac14+8\times\tfrac18=\tfrac{24}{8}=3.\)\par For $Z=(4X+1)/2$ the distribution is\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&0&1&2&3\\\hline z&0.5&2.5&4.5&6.5\\\hline \mathrm P(Z=z)&\frac14&\frac38&\frac14&\frac18\\\hline\end{array}\)\par \(\mathrm E(Z)=\sum_z z\mathrm P(Z=z)\)\par \(=0.5\times\tfrac14+2.5\times\tfrac38+4.5\times\tfrac14+6.5\times\tfrac18\)\par \(=0.125+0.9375+1.125+0.8125=3.\)\par Hence $\mathrm E(Y)=\mathrm E(Z)=3$.\par \textbf{c} $\mathrm E(Z^2)=\sum_z z^2\mathrm P(Z=z)$\par \(=0.5^2\times\tfrac14+2.5^2\times\tfrac38+4.5^2\times\tfrac14+6.5^2\times\tfrac18\)\par \(=0.0625+2.34375+5.0625+5.28125=12.75.\)\par \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\mathrm E(Z^2)-[\mathrm E(Z)]^2=12.75-3^2=3.75.\)\par Alternatively, $Z=(4X+1)/2=2X+0.5$.\par \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=2^2\operatorname{Var}(X)=4\times0.9375=3.75.\)

slides.title: Recovering the original mean and variance

transcription.tex: For a coding $Y=aX+b$ with $a\ne0$, we can recover the mean and variance of $X$ from those of $Y$.

$X$ is a discrete random variable. The discrete random variable $Y$ is defined as $Y=\dfrac{X-150}{50}$.\par Given that $\mathrm E(Y)=5.1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2.5$, find:\par \textbf{a} $\mathrm E(X)$\par \textbf{b} $\operatorname{Var}(X)$
$\mathrm E(Y)=\mathrm E\!\left(\dfrac{X-150}{50}\right)=\dfrac{\mathrm E(X)-150}{50}$.\par $\mathrm E(X)=50\times5.1+150=405$.
$\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\dfrac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{50^2}$.\par $\operatorname{Var}(X)=2.5\times50^2=6250$.

The discrete random variable \(X\) has a probability distribution given by\par \[\begin{array}{c|ccccc}x&-2&-1&0&1&2\\P\left(X=x\right)&0.3&a&0.25&b&c\end{array}\]\par The discrete random variable \(Y\) is defined as \(Y=3X-1\).\par Given that \(E\left(Y\right)=-2.5\) and \(Var\left(Y\right)=13.95\), find:\par \textbf{a} \(E(X)\) and \(E\left({X}^{2}\right)\)\par \textbf{b} the values of \(a, b\) and \(c\)\par \textbf{c} \(P\left(X>Y\right)\)

\(E(Y)=3E(X)-1\), so \(E(X)=(-2.5+1)/3=-0.5\).\par \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=9\operatorname{Var}(X)\), so \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=13.95/9=1.55\).\par \(E(X^2)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+E(X)^2=1.55+(-0.5)^2=1.8\).
Question 4

The discrete random variable $X$ has a probability distribution given by\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline x&90^\circ&180^\circ&270^\circ\\\hline \mathrm P(X=x)&a&b&0.3\\\hline\end{array}\)\par The random variable $Y$ is defined as $Y=\sin X^\circ$.\par \textbf{a} Find the range of possible values of $\mathrm E(Y)$.\par \textbf{b} Given that $\mathrm E(Y)=0.2$, write down the values of $a$ and $b$.

\textbf{a} The probability distribution of $Y$ is\par \(\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline y&1&0&-1\\\hline \mathrm P(Y=y)&a&b&0.3\\\hline\end{array}\)\par \(\mathrm E(Y)=a+0\times b-1\times0.3=a-0.3.\)\par Since $a+b+0.3=1$ and both probabilities are non-negative, $0\le a\le0.7$.\par At $a=0.7$, $\mathrm E(Y)=0.4$. At $a=0$, $\mathrm E(Y)=-0.3$.\par \(-0.3\le\mathrm E(Y)\le0.4.\)\par \textbf{b} $\mathrm E(Y)=0.2$ gives $0.2=a-0.3$, so $a=0.5$.\par The probabilities sum to 1. Hence $a+b+0.3=1$, giving $b=1-0.3-0.5=0.2$.
Question 6

The discrete random variable $X$ has a probability distribution given by\par \(\mathrm P(X=x)=\begin{cases}a&x=1,2,3\\ b&x=4,5\\ c&x=6\end{cases}\)\par Suppose that $Y$ is defined by $Y=1-2X$.\par \textbf{a} Given that $\mathrm E(Y)=-5.6$ and $\mathrm P(Y\le-5)=0.6$, write down the value of $\mathrm E(X)$.\par \textbf{b} Show that:\par \(\begin{aligned}3a+2b+c&=1\\2a+3b+2c&=1.1\\a+2b+c&=0.6\end{aligned}\)\par \textbf{c} Solve the system to find values for $a$, $b$, $c$.\par \textbf{d} Find $\mathrm P(X>5+Y)$.

\textbf{a} $\mathrm E(Y)=\mathrm E(1-2X)=1-2\mathrm E(X)$.\par \(-5.6=1-2\mathrm E(X)\quad\Rightarrow\quad 2\mathrm E(X)=6.6\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathrm E(X)=3.3.\)\par Alternatively, $Y=1-2X$ gives $X=\tfrac12-\tfrac Y2$.\par \(\mathrm E(X)=\mathrm E(\tfrac12-\tfrac Y2)=\tfrac12-\tfrac12\mathrm E(Y)=0.5-(-2.8)=3.3.\)\par \textbf{b} The probabilities sum to 1, so $a+a+a+b+b+c=1$.\par \(3a+2b+c=1\quad(1)\)\par From (a), $\mathrm E(X)=3.3$, so\par \(1a+2a+3a+4b+5b+6c=3.3.\)\par \(6a+9b+6c=3.3\quad\Rightarrow\quad 2a+3b+2c=1.1\quad(2)\)\par $Y\le-5$ means $1-2X\le-5$, or $X\ge3$. Thus $\mathrm P(Y\le-5)=\mathrm P(X\ge3)=0.6$.\par \(a+2b+c=0.6\quad(3)\)\par \textbf{c} $(1)-(3)$ gives $2a=0.4$, hence $a=0.2$.\par $2\times(3)$ gives $2a+4b+2c=1.2\quad(4)$.\par $(4)-(2)$ gives $b=0.1$. Substitute $a$ and $b$ in (3):\par \(0.2+0.2+c=0.6\quad\Rightarrow\quad c=0.2.\)\par Hence $a=0.2$, $b=0.1$, $c=0.2$.\par \textbf{d} Since $Y=1-2X$, $X>5+Y$ means $X>5+1-2X$, so $3X>6$ and $X>2$.\par \(\mathrm P(X>5+Y)=\mathrm P(X>2)=a+2b+c=0.2+2\times0.1+0.2=0.6.\)
